introduction-moving-beyond-hello-world.core: Terraform is a declarative reconciliation engine. You describe the desired end state in HCL, Terraform reads the real state through providers, diffs the two, and builds a dependency graph of create, update and delete actions. Moving beyond hello world means treating that loop (write → plan → apply → state) as a production system with modules, remote state, locking and review.

first_principles.problem: A team's single main.tf works on one laptop but breaks when three engineers apply at once.
truths: Real state must be read and remembered.
Changes are a diff, executed in dependency order.

analogy.title: An architect's blueprint and a builder
analogy.story: You hand over the blueprint; the builder compares it with the site, lists what to build or demolish, and does it in a safe order.
analogy.breaks: Builders improvise; Terraform does exactly what the plan says.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Exactly the reviewed plan is applied.

code.text:
terraform init      # download providers, configure backend
terraform plan -out=tf.plan
terraform show tf.plan   # review
terraform apply tf.plan

check.q: Why apply a saved plan file instead of running apply directly?
check.a: It guarantees that what's applied is exactly what was reviewed, with no new drift sneaking in between.

providers-the-bridge-to-the-cloud.core: Terraform core knows nothing about AWS or GitHub. Providers are plugins that translate resource CRUD into API calls. You pin their versions with required_providers and a lock file, configure credentials and region, and use aliases for multiple accounts or regions. Provider upgrades can change behaviour, so they are versioned like any dependency.

first_principles.problem: An unpinned provider auto-upgrades in CI and suddenly wants to replace every S3 bucket.

analogy.title: Travel adapters
analogy.story: Your laptop (core) works anywhere, but needs the right plug adapter for each country's sockets.
analogy.breaks: Adapters don't change behaviour; provider upgrades can.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Pinned version, two regions, one config.

check.a: Everyone and CI use the exact same provider versions and checksums selected at init.

data-sources-querying-reality.core: Data sources read existing information without managing it: the latest AMI, an existing VPC by tag, the current account ID, or outputs of another stack. They let configurations adapt to the world instead of hardcoding IDs. They are read on every plan, so a broad or changing query can cause surprising diffs.

first_principles.problem: Hardcoded AMI and subnet IDs break when code is reused in another account.
truths: Some resources exist outside this config.

analogy.title: Looking up a phone number instead of memorising it
analogy.story: You query the directory each time, so the number stays right even if it changes.
analogy.breaks: Directories are stable; a 'latest AMI' query changes every week.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Same code works in every account that owns golden images.

check.q: Why can a 'most_recent' AMI data source cause instance replacement?
check.a: A new AMI changes the value on the next plan, and changing an instance's AMI forces replacement.

modules-the-lego-blocks.core: A module is a directory of Terraform with inputs (variables) and outputs, called with source and version. Modules encapsulate a pattern, such as a VPC or a service, so teams reuse tested building blocks instead of copying resources. Good modules have a small, typed interface, sensible defaults, versioned releases and no hidden provider configuration.

first_principles.problem: Twelve copies of the same VPC code have drifted apart, each with different bugs.

analogy.title: LEGO bricks
analogy.story: Standard studs (interfaces) let any brick connect, and you build castles from tested pieces instead of carving wood each time.
analogy.breaks: LEGO never changes; modules release versions with breaking changes.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Tested VPC with one block, upgradeable by bumping version.

check.q: Why shouldn't child modules declare provider blocks?
check.a: It prevents callers from controlling configuration (regions, aliases) and blocks using for_each/count on the module.

loops-count-vs-for_each.core: count creates N indexed copies (resource[0], resource[1]); for_each creates copies keyed by map or set values (resource["web"]). Because count identifies instances by position, removing an item in the middle shifts indexes and destroys and recreates everything after it. for_each keys are stable, so use count only for on/off toggles or truly identical replicas.

first_principles.problem: Removing the second user from a list of 10 IAM users makes Terraform plan to recreate 8 of them.
truths: Instance addresses come from index or key.
derivation: Use **for_each** with maps/sets of stable keys.

analogy.title: Seat numbers vs name cards
analogy.story: If guests sit by seat number and one leaves, everyone shuffles along; with name cards, nobody moves.
analogy.breaks: Guests shuffle harmlessly; resources get destroyed.

check.q: When is count still the right choice?
check.a: For conditional creation (0 or 1) or truly interchangeable replicas where position doesn't matter.

environment-separation-workspaces-vs-dir.core: CLI workspaces give one configuration several state files (dev, prod) selected at runtime, which is easy but invisible: the same code, backend and credentials, with a single wrong `workspace select` hitting prod. Directory-per-environment gives each environment its own root module, backend and variables. That is more duplication, but explicit, separately permissioned, and able to diverge safely.

first_principles.problem: An engineer runs apply thinking they're in dev but the workspace is prod.
derivation: Give each env its own **backend and credentials**.

analogy.title: Tabs in one spreadsheet vs separate files
analogy.story: Tabs are quick but you can edit the wrong one; separate files in separate folders with different locks are harder to confuse.
analogy.breaks: Spreadsheets have undo; prod deletions don't.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: prod uses a different bucket and role; dev credentials can't touch it.

code.text:
envs/
  dev/   main.tf  backend.tf  terraform.tfvars
  prod/  main.tf  backend.tf  terraform.tfvars
modules/
  service/

check.q: Where are CLI workspaces a good fit?
check.a: Short-lived identical copies, like per-branch preview environments, where implicit selection is low risk.

state-locking-preventing-disaster.core: Two concurrent applies against the same state can both read version N, make conflicting changes, and write competing versions, corrupting state or orphaning resources. Backends with locking (S3 with a DynamoDB table or native S3 lockfile, GCS, Terraform Cloud) take an exclusive lock for the whole run. A stuck lock is released with force-unlock, only after confirming no run is active.

first_principles.problem: Two CI jobs apply simultaneously and the state file loses track of a newly created database.
derivation: Hold the lock for the **whole run**.

analogy.title: A single key to the records room
analogy.story: Only the key holder may edit the ledger; others wait at the door.
analogy.breaks: Keys can't get stuck in a crashed process; locks can.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Second apply waits or fails with 'state locked'.

check.q: What should you check before running terraform force-unlock?
check.a: That no apply is actually still running (CI job, colleague), otherwise you reintroduce concurrent writes.

provisioners-the-avoid-feature.core: Provisioners (local-exec, remote-exec, file) run scripts during create or destroy. HashiCorp calls them a last resort because Terraform can't model what they do: their effects aren't in state, they aren't idempotent, failures taint resources, and they need network and SSH access during apply. Prefer cloud-init/user_data, baked images, configuration management or native resources.

first_principles.problem: A remote-exec provisioner fails halfway, the instance is tainted, and the next apply destroys a half-configured server.

analogy.title: Duct tape on a blueprint
analogy.story: It holds something together, but the blueprint no longer describes the building.
analogy.breaks: Duct tape is visible; provisioner effects are invisible to state.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Boot config runs on the instance; Terraform stays declarative.

check.q: What happens to a resource if a creation-time provisioner fails?
check.a: It is marked tainted and will be destroyed and recreated on the next apply.

preconditions-and-postconditions-asserti.core: Variable validation checks inputs. lifecycle precondition blocks check assumptions before a resource is planned, postcondition blocks check guarantees after it's created or read, and check blocks run continuous assertions that warn without failing. Together they turn tribal knowledge ("this AMI must be x86", "the bucket must be encrypted") into executable contracts with clear error messages.

first_principles.problem: Someone passes an ARM AMI to an x86 instance type and the failure only shows up as a vague API error after 10 minutes.

analogy.title: Pre-flight and post-landing checklists
analogy.story: Pilots verify conditions before take-off and confirm state after landing, catching problems at the cheapest moment.
analogy.breaks: Pilots can override; failed conditions halt the run.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Mismatch caught at plan with a readable message.

check.q: How does a check block differ from a postcondition?
check.a: A failed check block produces a warning without stopping the run; a failed postcondition is an error that halts it.

opentofu-the-open-source-fork.core: In 2023 HashiCorp relicensed Terraform under the Business Source License, and the community forked the last MPL version as OpenTofu under the Linux Foundation. OpenTofu stays largely compatible with Terraform 1.5-era configs and state while adding its own features, such as client-side state encryption and early variable evaluation. The choice is about licence, governance, ecosystem and feature roadmap.

first_principles.problem: A company building an internal platform worries that Terraform's BSL licence restricts its use.
truths: State and HCL compatibility ease migration.
derivation: Use the **OpenTofu registry** mirror of providers.
Pin the **binary** in CI (tofu vs terraform).

analogy.title: A recipe book going proprietary
analogy.story: The community photocopies the last free edition and keeps adding recipes; old dishes still cook the same.
analogy.breaks: Recipes don't need compatibility; state files do.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Zero-diff plan proves compatibility before switching.

code.text:
tofu init        # reads same backend and lock file
tofu plan        # expect: No changes
# then swap 'terraform' for 'tofu' in CI

check.q: What's a safe first check when migrating a stack to OpenTofu?
check.a: Run tofu init and plan against the existing state and confirm it shows no changes.
